title: How our TDD loop works now
desc: The whole build loop in plain English, with the new review rules folded in. Two workers on purpose: Feature Tickets writes the test + cleans the code + owns the PR; Green Pass only makes it pass — you can't game a test you didn't write. Per ticket: RED (Feature Tickets writes an honest failing test first — checks inputs/outputs not the guts, no cheat-tests) → GREEN (Green Pass makes it really pass, smallest change, no faking) → REFACTOR (Feature Tickets tidies against a fixed list of 12 'code smells' — cleanup #1, in the loop). Then CHECK TWICE before the PR: Clean? (the 12 smells) + Right? (does exactly what the ticket asked) — cleanup #2. THE GATE: batch up to 5 tickets, Greptile scores it, 5/5 auto-merges to staging; stuck below 5/5 → 7 tries → split → escalate to you. Only you promote staging → main, with a passing test + your yes. Cleanup happens both in the loop and at the gate; the test stays honest from the first red.

title: Who actually does the code review?
desc: I took the portable parts of Matt Pocock's code-review method and wired them into the build loop. Two new rules: a two-way check on every change (Clean? — against a fixed list of 12 'code smells'; Right? — does exactly what the ticket asked, no more) and honest tests (no fake pass, no peeking at insides, no test that breaks on tidy-up). Your catch: a rule everyone can see is nobody's job — the rulebook reached all 10 seats as background but told no worker it was theirs. Fixed by handing the job to the two seats that do the work: Feature Tickets (honest reds, clean against the smells, two-way self-check before the PR) and Green Pass (make it really pass, no faking). Tester and Front-end left out for now. All in 2 pull requests, not merged — your yes needed. Two decisions for you: keep clean-up in both build+review or move to review only; and whether to wire the other 2 seats.

title: Is it really set up — and does it actually work?
desc: You asked me to be sure the delegation-manager was actually installed, and whether the 'hand each teammate their rulebook' step is a real working thing or just something I read in the manual. So I checked by running it. First find: it was NOT really installed — the tool's own note about where it lives pointed at a scratch folder the computer had already thrown away, so typing its name would have done nothing. I installed it for real, and the built-in health check (the 'doctor') now says OK to every line. Then the injection: I ran the tool and it printed the actual rulebook it would hand one teammate, and for the manager it added the manager's kickoff instructions on top — exactly as promised. Its own tests all pass (120 of them), and the helper that finds each teammate's screen works right now. The one thing I did not do, on purpose: fire the very last step that pushes the rulebook onto a live teammate's screen — because the only room I'm standing in is the real DMS team's room, and I won't poke a working team. Everything up to that final push is proven live.

title: How a new team gets the template
desc: The plain-English version of how a brand-new team starts using the template. The template is a 'starter kit' — a set of empty folders, one per job, with blanks that say <TEAM> where the name goes. One command does the rest: it makes a fresh private notebook just for that team, photocopies the starter kit into it (one folder per job — manager, the two planners, researcher, tester, and the rest), writes the real team name into every <TEAM> blank, adds a shared handoff tray for half-finished tasks, saves and uploads the notebook to the team's own private place online, then checks its own homework and stops loudly if any blank was left empty. The big thing to understand: it's a photocopy, not a live feed — the team gets a snapshot of the template exactly as it looks the moment they're created, and after that they work from their own copy. Change the template later and that team doesn't automatically get it; someone has to hand them an update. (The folders mostly hold sticky-notes pointing to the shared rulebook, not the rules themselves — those come down a separate pipe.)

File 1 DEPARTMENTS.md (the little map listing each department, its branch, and what it owns): a status word went from 'wave-N' to 'queued', plus a new line '2 or more sections = a big project'. File 2 manager-global-rules.md (the rulebook every team follows): added 'split into as many sections as the plan needs, no cap' and rewrote the crew rule to '3 crews at once (core + 2)'. File 3 merging.md (how each department's branch joins the shared branch): the same crew-count fix. They were never approved, so they sit untouched waiting for your yes. Your 1 decision: commit these 3 wording files to staging as their own separate commit — yes or no.

title: What we've actually built (mirror map)
desc: A like-for-like map of the real DMS repository — exactly what's built, named part by part. 1) The Manager (the brain): the OMP skill you talk to (SKILL.md, manager/PROMPT.md, WORKFLOW.md, config.yml) — drives everything, checks the work, never builds itself. 2) The planning pipeline (fixed order): draft-one.sh merges two blind drafts → launch-first-goal.sh (Plannotator) → launch-wayfinder.sh → final goal → PRD, and dispatch.sh blocks building until the final plan is approved. 3) Teams and their memory: new-team-memory.sh gives each team a private notebook of 10 seats (changelog/knowledge/state per seat), upgrade-team.sh updates old teams, and the Manager writes with record-change / remember. 4) Getting rules into every pane: sync-global-rules.sh pulls the one shared rulebook, pane-inject.sh loads it plus each role's prompt into its pane, comms.py guarantees a message hits exactly one pane and never bleeds into another team's tab. 5) The Operations Manager: ops-manager.sh creates it the moment a team exists, ops-clock.sh fires timed report nudges (status, pre-block, end-of-block) and the refresh that pushes new rules to every team. 6) Departments → one codebase: big plans split into departments (templates/department/, DEPARTMENTS.md), each on its own branch, reassembling dept → central staging → main; dept-close.sh closes finished panes but keeps the branch + history. 7) The tested core underneath: the delegation_manager Python package (ops, comms, memory, CLI) with 120 checks passing across 11 test suites, install.sh to set up and doctor.sh to health-check.

title: How it all works now (the map)
desc: The whole system in one map, top to bottom — and the fix to a common mix-up: an idea does NOT start with Ops. 1) Your idea goes straight from you to the core Manager, one-on-one, never through Ops; the whole planning stage is just you and the manager. 2) Get set up to plan: together you pick the language, name the repo, decide what's needed, Research prices it, and you approve the cost + setup before any planning starts. 3) The plan gets written and approved: two planners draft it (blind, then merged) through two Plannotator checkpoints with Wayfinder between; you approve the facts then the plan at each — four approvals — giving the Gold Plan + PRD. 4) Cut into sections: the approved plan splits into as many sections as it needs (no limit), each section a department; one section needs no department, the core team builds it. 5) Three crews at a time: only 3 teams run at once (core + 2), the rest queue, one out one in. 6) NOW Ops is the switchboard: while teams build, reports and day-to-day decisions go team → Ops → you and back (planning always stays direct). 7) It all comes together: each piece rolls up team → central staging → main into one codebase (main needs your OK), and a rule change reaches everyone when you tell Ops 'push'.

title: Who inherits what?
desc: When a team starts — or gets updated — 'inherit' hides a split. Three separate things travel at different speeds. RULES: a rule change reaches a new team AND the running teams (SM, HAP) automatically — that's the refresh, on your word. TOOLKIT + CODE: a brand-new team is built from the shared master copy, so it gets every tool and every bit of code finished so far; but SM and HAP copied the toolkit when they started, so new tools built later do NOT reach them on their own — someone has to pull them in (no background robot does it). PRIVATE NOTES: never travel — each team keeps its own private notebook, a new team starts empty and fresh, nobody inherits another team's notes. One decision inside: should toolkit updates auto-reach running teams too, or stay a deliberate manual pull? (I lean manual for now — rules are safe to auto-send, code isn't.)

title: Who cuts up the plan?
desc: Who splits the Gold Plan + PRD into sections and breaks them into phases? Departments are lean with no planners, so they never slice or phase their own work — they get their part already cut and already phased. Two layers: planners set the section/phase boundaries; each team's Feature Tickets seat fills each phase with the actual tickets.
